questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: A key factor in choosing my study destination was finding a university with strong expertise in persuasive technologies and behavioural design. I was also drawn to the opportunity for interdisciplinary collaboration between cognition and communication—an essential foundation for my academic and professional goals. Additionally, I valued a location that offered good weather, access to outdoor activities, and strong sports and fitness opportunities to support a balanced lifestyle during my exchange.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
I truly valued the academic experience I had; however, my first quarter was extremely challenging due to bureaucratic obstacles that initially prevented me from living with other graduate students and enrolling in graduate-level courses. As an older student (33), I unfortunately faced discrimination and hostility from the undergraduate students I was housed with. Their priorities were centered around partying and socializing, which starkly contrasted with my academic responsibilities and lifestyle.

This conflict escalated when they knowingly acquired a cat despite my documented allergy and began publicly targeting me with bullying on platforms like Reddit. They also repeatedly accused me of things I hadn’t done, leading to multiple five-hour mediation meetings with our RA that unfortunately only resulted in further gaslighting and emotional distress. These circumstances severely impacted both my physical and mental health and had a significant negative effect on my academic performance and overall well-being during the first quarter.

After many exhausting hours spent navigating various departments—from the Ombuds Office and social workers to multiple housing offices—I was eventually approved to relocate to graduate housing. This transition dramatically improved my living situation and had a profoundly positive impact on the rest of my exchange experience.

Additionally, the overall communication and coordination between UCSB and the University of Copenhagen (KU) could have been improved. Although KU informed me that, despite the exchange agreement being at the undergraduate level, it was common practice to allow students to enroll in at least one graduate-level course, UCSB expressed confusion and told me I was the first student they had to support in this regard. Fortunately, I received excellent support from the administrative staff in both the Communication and Psychology departments.

That said, I experienced ongoing challenges navigating UCSB’s complex and highly bureaucratic structure. It was often unclear who to contact for specific issues, which led to confusion and delays in resolving problems. Communication with the EAP office was particularly difficult, as my assigned contact person was only available on certain days and often had long response times—making it harder to receive timely support when needed.

Socially, I also found the experience quite isolating. As a graduate student, it was difficult to connect with peers. Most UCSB graduate students work in established lab groups or co-ops, which left little room for informal networking or new social connections. Without structured opportunities to meet others in a similar situation, I often felt quite alone during the initial stages of my exchange.

Furthermore, the lack of a proper introduction or orientation to UCSB’s academic support systems made it difficult to access important resources early on. I was unaware of crucial tools such as the Disabled Students Program (DSP) (I have post concussion syndrome and ADHD) and was only able to apply for accommodations at the very last minute before my exams. Similarly, I didn’t discover helpful services like CLAS tutoring or exam preparation sessions until late in the first quarter—support that could have made a meaningful difference if accessed earlier.

That said, I was also extremely grateful for individual professors who went above and beyond to support my academic journey. Their flexibility, understanding, and genuine encouragement played a crucial role in helping me succeed despite the obstacles.

Despite the early challenges, I’m grateful for the resilience I developed and the academic and personal growth I experienced throughout the exchange.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was quite difficult to find the information I needed upon arrival. Many processes were unclear, and I lacked proper guidance on where to go or who to contact for specific issues. Without a structured introduction or orientation tailored to exchange or graduate students, I struggled to navigate essential systems such as housing, class registration, and academic support services. Much of the information I eventually found was through trial and error or after receiving help from individual staff members or departments later in the quarter.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There was an introductory gathering organized by EAP, where we received a folder with some of the most essential information. While this was helpful as a starting point, I found that a lot of important details were missing—particularly regarding academic procedures, available support services, and how to navigate the university as a graduate-level exchange student. As a DSP student, I especially would have benefited from earlier guidance on how to access accommodations and support, as this information was not clearly communicated.

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
Housing is generally difficult to secure and very expensive off campus, which can be a major source of stress for incoming students. I was fortunate to be selected through the lottery for off-campus university housing. However, as mentioned earlier, my initial placement with undergraduate students was extremely difficult and not well-suited to my needs as a graduate exchange student. The living situation caused significant challenges for me, my housemates, and the housing facilities. I strongly believe that all parties would have benefited if I had been assigned to graduate housing from the beginning, where the environment is better aligned with the lifestyle and responsibilities of graduate-level students.
I only discovered alternative housing options through different landlords and UCSB-affiliated agencies midway through my exchange. It would have been very helpful to receive this information earlier. A dedicated meeting or orientation session outlining housing options, including off-campus partners and graduate housing opportunities, at the beginning of the program would have made a big difference

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
Future exchange students should know that living off campus can be both expensive and competitive, especially in Isla Vista and the surrounding areas. Start your housing search as early as possible, and be prepared for high rent prices and shared living situations—often in shared bedrooms.

Housing in Isla Vista is very different from what many are used to in places like Copenhagen, where you typically find housemates based on personal compatibility. In IV, you’re often assigned a spot—sometimes just a bed in a shared room—without knowing anything about the people you’ll be living with. It can feel like a bit of a lottery whether you end up with housemates you’re compatible with or not. You should also be prepared to move more than once, often in the middle of a quarter, if the living situation turns out to be unsustainable. Also, ask early about UCSB-affiliated landlords or agencies, as they may offer more structured and reliable options that aren’t always clearly communicated upfront.

If you're a graduate student, try to request graduate housing or ask specifically about options that are better suited for academic life. 

Finally, don’t hesitate to advocate for yourself if your housing situation isn’t working—support systems do exist, but they can take persistence and time to access.

How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
The registration process itself—through the GOLD system—is fairly straightforward. However, I would have appreciated more guidance early on about how to navigate course waitlists and the process for sitting in on classes.

My main advice to future exchange students is to be very aware of your assigned registration time, as it may occur during the night if you're in Europe, and popular classes fill up quickly. Sign up for as many courses as possible initially—you can always drop them later—and plan to sit in on several during the first week.

Since course descriptions online are often very limited, attending the first class is often the only way to get a sense of the content, expectations, and teaching style. Be prepared for a chaotic first week, where you may need to juggle your schedule, arrive late, or leave early to sit in on multiple overlapping classes.

Also, if you're on a waitlist, it’s crucial to attend the class from day one. Many instructors will automatically drop students who are waitlisted but don’t show up, so don’t assume you're safe unless you've been officially added to the roster.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Not a lot to be honest. Try to ask your local classmates.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Although I missed my original registration deadline, I was fortunate to secure the classes I wanted by staying active on waitlists and proactively reaching out to professors.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Remember that in the U.S., professors typically hold a great deal of autonomy over their courses and are the ones who decide whether exceptions or modifications can be made. If you encounter any issues, reach out to them directly—and early. Clear, respectful communication often goes a long way. It’s also a good idea to schedule a meeting with the administrative staff in your department early on; they can be incredibly helpful when it comes to navigating course enrollment, waitlists, and academic procedures.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
Overall, I was satisfied with the academic programme at my host institution. UCSB offers a broad range of courses, and I appreciated the opportunity to explore subjects aligned with my academic interests—particularly in communication, psychology, and cognitive science.

That said, the quality and depth of learning varied considerably depending on class size and the teaching style of individual professors. Some undergraduate courses felt less academically rigorous compared to what I’m used to in Denmark, often relying on memorization and multiple-choice exams. However, I found the smaller, discussion-based seminars and graduate-level courses to be far more intellectually engaging.

The ability to sit in on classes and directly connect with professors was a major advantage. Once I navigated the initial administrative hurdles, I was able to tailor my course selection to better support my academic goals. While the academic environment wasn’t quite what I expected, I still gained a great deal—both intellectually and personally. It took me about a quarter to fully adapt to the structure and expectations, so I would highly recommend staying for more than one quarter if possible, to make the most of the experience.

One particular highlight was the flexibility some professors showed in allowing me to modify undergraduate assignments to reflect graduate-level expectations. In several cases, this meant writing analytical essays connected to my field of interest instead of completing standard multiple-choice exams. I also greatly enjoyed the opportunity to engage in independent studies, which allowed for deeper, self-directed exploration of topics I’m passionate about.

For courses that do rely on multiple-choice assessments, I recommend paying close attention to how professors frame their material. Often, the 'correct' answers reflect the instructor’s particular interpretation or emphasis, which can introduce a degree of bias. Understanding their perspective early on can make a big difference in how well you perform.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
The academic level at UCSB varies significantly depending on the professor, department, and class size. Class formats range from small seminars with 5 students to large lectures with over 500, each offering very different learning experiences. Smaller, seminar-style classes tend to promote intellectual engagement, discussion, and critical thinking, while larger undergraduate courses often rely on multiple-choice exams and emphasize factual recall over deeper understanding.

In my experience, many undergraduate classes focused more on how much information you could memorize rather than how well you could analyze or apply it. This approach felt quite similar to high school, especially when compared to my Danish BA and MA education, which is typically more discussion-driven and encourages independent thinking and critical analysis.

To make the most of the academic experience at UCSB, I strongly recommend reviewing course syllabi carefully, speaking directly with professors about their learning objectives, and, when possible, prioritizing upper-division or smaller classes. Not only will this help clarify expectations, but direct communication also increases the chance of building a supportive relationship with your instructor, which can be very beneficial

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
The teaching style at UCSB differed quite significantly from what I’m used to at the University of Copenhagen. In Denmark, courses tend to be more discussion-based, with a strong emphasis on critical thinking, independent analysis, and active student participation. Assessments often involve written essays and oral exams that require you to develop and defend your perspective.

At UCSB—particularly in larger undergraduate courses—the teaching style was more lecture-driven, with a focus on memorization and multiple-choice exams. While some classes encouraged engagement, the overall structure felt more passive and content-heavy. That said, I found smaller seminars and independent study options more aligned with the academic environment I’m used to in Copenhagen. I also appreciated the flexibility some professors offered in adapting assignments to better match graduate-level expectations.

One important thing to be aware of is that professors at UCSB are often leading experts in their specific research fields. While this is a great opportunity to learn from top scholars, their deep specialization can sometimes introduce bias in how content is taught and assessed—particularly in classes where multiple-choice exams reflect the professor’s particular interpretation of the material. Understanding their academic lens and expectations early on is key to succeeding and making the most of the course

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I truly enjoyed all of my classes, especially because I had a well-balanced combination of communication, psychology, and acting courses that personally suited me very well.

Academically, I learned the most from PSY 163BG – The Active Brain. Professor Giesbrecht is an excellent facilitator of knowledge, and I really appreciated both his teaching style and the structure of the course. I also gained a great deal from working with Professor Rice. I was fortunate to take COMM 199 – Independent Studies as an extension of our collaboration in COMM 163 – Diffusion of Innovations. It was incredibly rewarding to continue developing my project in more depth during the second quarter.

On a personal level, the acting classes were also a powerful part of my experience. They helped me reflect on the psychological concepts I was learning and apply them in new, creative ways. These classes pushed my personal boundaries, encouraged emotional growth, and gave me a much-needed ‘off-screen’ playground for self-expression and development.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Be proactive and flexible about both course registration and social groups.
Courses fill up quickly, and the system can be confusing at first—especially if you're in a different time zone. Sign up for as many classes as you can initially (you can always drop them later), sit in on multiple classes the first week, and don’t hesitate to contact professors directly—especially if you're waitlisted. The same goes for social life: finding your community takes initiative, especially as a graduate student. Explore clubs, dance classes, or fitness groups early, and don’t be afraid to show up alone—you often have to make the first move.

2. Prepare for a different academic culture and structure.
The quarter system moves very fast and can feel very intense. Do not fall behind early on—you simply won’t have time to catch up later. Many undergraduate courses rely heavily on memorization and multiple-choice exams rather than critical thinking and discussion. Try to choose smaller or upper-division classes, and if you're a graduate student, speak with professors about adapting assignments to a more advanced level. Independent studies can also be a great way to tailor your learning experience.

3. Don’t underestimate the housing challenge.
Housing in Isla Vista is expensive, competitive, and often shared with undergrads in a party-heavy environment. If you're a grad student, push early for graduate housing or explore UCSB-affiliated landlords. Be prepared to move—possibly more than once—and expect little control over who you live with. If you don’t get housing through UCSB, expect to pay between 7,000 and 15,000 DKK per month to share a room with up to four people in Isla Vista. The experience can vary a lot depending on your living situation, so advocate for your needs early.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: get a car if you can or at least a bike public transportation is pretty bad. Often the busses are full during primetime and they only goes a couple of times an hour.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer:
The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was the personal and academic growth that came from navigating a completely new system and environment. While there were many challenges—especially in the beginning—they pushed me to become more proactive, adaptable, and resilient.

Academically, I was especially grateful for the opportunity to tailor some of my coursework to fit my research interests and to collaborate with inspiring professors. For me, it was a unique opportunity to combine classes from psychology, communication, and acting (theater)—a combination that allowed me to explore human behavior from both scientific and expressive perspectives.

Personally, I also really enjoyed exploring California. I’m more of a city girl, so I found it quite difficult to adjust to life in Isla Vista, which felt isolated and very student-party oriented. But traveling around the state was an incredible highlight—I absolutely loved San Francisco, Napa Valley, Lake Tahoe, San Diego, and especially my dream spot, Venice Beach.

The mix of academic stimulation and personal adventure made the exchange a truly transformative experience.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
The greatest challenge during my exchange was the living situation in the first quarter. As a graduate student, I was placed in housing with undergraduate students whose priorities and lifestyles were very different from mine. This created ongoing conflicts, including severe allergic reactions when they knowingly brought a cat into the shared space, as well as social tension and even public bullying online.

Navigating the housing bureaucracy to find a solution was extremely time-consuming and emotionally draining. It affected both my mental health and academic performance during that quarter. However, once I was finally relocated to graduate housing, my experience improved dramatically.

This situation taught me a lot about advocating for myself, setting boundaries, and navigating complex systems—skills I know I’ll carry with me moving forward.
